title: Guru Angad close
hook: the second Guru taught the script, the body and a few sharp lines

segments.voice: Yesterday, haumai, ego: a long, deep illness, with its medicine inside it. Your line was the cure inside. When the I got loud, did you catch it, even once? Today we close our stretch with Guru Angad. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

A patch of packed earth where young men wrestle in the early morning, dust on their shoulders. A page of letters copied out in a careful, rounded hand. A long row of people sitting on the floor, being handed bowls of rice pudding. And a handful of short verses, tucked into the ballads of the Granth. Four pictures, one life. Tradition connects each of them to Guru Angad, the quiet successor. Today we gather them up: the script, the body, the kitchen, and the few sharp lines.
screen: `A WRESTLING GROUND, A PAGE OF LETTERS.` → `A ROW OF BOWLS.` → `A FEW SHORT VERSES.`

segments.voice: Start with the letters. Tradition says Guru Angad gave shape to the Gurmukhi script and taught it, so that ordinary people could read and write the Gurus' words in their own language. Then the body. Tradition says he set up wrestling grounds at Khadur and encouraged exercise and strength. A healthy body, in this telling, isn't a distraction from the spiritual life; it's part of a life that can serve. Then the kitchen. Here the Granth itself speaks. In a ballad by the bards Satta and Balvand, his wife, Mata Khivi, is praised, in paraphrase, as a good woman who gives shade like a tree full of leaves. In the langar, it says, wealth is shared out, and rice pudding with ghee is served, sweet as nectar. And then the lines themselves, the ones we've spent four days on. See without eyes, walk without feet. A hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru. Service spoiled by pride. Ego as a long illness, with its medicine inside. Put it all together and a style shows. Nothing wasted. A script so people could read. A body kept ready. A kitchen that feeds. And verses so short they fit in the palm of your hand, and so sharp they still cut through. That's what the second Guru left: not volume, but edge. That's today's line.
screen: `THE LETTERS: GURMUKHI TAUGHT.` · `THE BODY: WRESTLING AT KHADUR.` · `THE KITCHEN: MATA KHIVI'S LANGAR.` · `THE LINES: SHORT, AND STILL CUTTING.` · then, large: `SHORT AND SHARP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one sharp line. In the sit, let the breath slow, and let this week's pictures pass by: the muddy grass, the hundred moons, the illness with its cure. Ask what one thing you've learned lately, about your work, your people, or yourself, and try to say it in a single short sentence. Cut a word. Then another. When it's as short as it can be, hold it on the breath. Write it down after the bell if you like. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Guru Angad close. The second Guru: tradition credits him with the script and the wrestling ground, the Granth praises Mata Khivi's langar, and his saloks are few lines that cut deep. Today's word.
Your line: short and sharp. Keep the sentence you wrote, and read it once more before you sleep. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Angad in the ardas and on his gurpurab, read his saloks within the Vars, and tell of Mata Khivi's langar when they speak of the free kitchen's history.

notes: Editor pass: the child's-slate opener repeated day 1176's 'child's writing tablet', so the hook now opens on the wrestling ground and a page of letters; cut the unsourced claim that the Patti's letters are the ones Guru Angad taught (historians debate how far the script predates him).
Guru Angad's role in shaping and teaching Gurmukhi is given as 'tradition says' (historians discuss how far the script predates him); please confirm the wording.
The wrestling grounds (mall akhara) at Khadur are given as tradition; please confirm.

The Satta and Balvand lines on Mata Khivi ('Balvand Khivi nek jan jis bahutee chhaau patraalee; langar daulat vandeeai ras amrit kheer ghiaalee') are paraphrased and placed at Ang 967; please confirm.
'The second Guru' and 'four days' refer to Mahala two and days 1177–1180 respectively.
